title: Replayable Conversation Consumer & Local Test Harness for Python SDK Streaming
creator: Asha Patel
description:
This ticket proposes a reusable, testable pattern and developer-facing primitives for deterministic local testing of streaming chat completions and event handling in the Python SDK. The main deliverable is a Replayable Conversation Consumer (RCC) and a small local harness that can: 1) record real streaming sessions (token/event timeline and timing), 2) replay them deterministically in unit/integration tests, and 3) inject controlled network/backpressure/cancellation events to validate retry and resume behaviors. The goal is to reduce flakiness in CI tests for streaming features and to provide a clear example for customers who need to validate resume, retries, and handler-side idempotency.

Why different from existing work: many of our streaming tickets focus on runtime-level ergonomics (iterators, checkpoints, adapters). This work targets the developer/testing surface: a library + fixtures that make it straightforward to assert correct behavior under real-world streaming failures without running GPUs or the full service. It also codifies event schemas and deterministic timing semantics so our tests and examples are reproducible across platforms.
acceptance_criteria: A small Python package (redwood_sdk.replay) implements a record/replay harness usable from pytest
A Replayable Conversation Consumer API that accepts recorded timelines and yields the same event objects with preserved inter-event timing
Unit tests that simulate mid-stream network disconnects and verify the SDK's retry + resume logic against the harness
A design doc and example notebook demonstrating how to capture a live session and use it as a deterministic fixture
CI integration: at least two flaky streaming tests replaced with replay-based variants showing >90% reduction in flakiness
design_notes:
Core primitives: (1) Recorder: lightweight middleware that serializes a sequence of events with precise timestamps and optional debug metadata; (2) Replayer: an async generator that emits events according to the recorded timing, supports speedup/stretch factors, and can inject network errors or suspend for backpressure semantics; (3) Event Normalizer: maps live events to a stable schema for equality assertions; (4) CancellationToken and Clock abstraction: allows tests to fast-forward or freeze time without sleeping. The harness must not be tied to runtime internals (no private protobufs) so it can be published to customers as a test utility.

Event schema decisions: adopt a small, typed set of event kinds we already emit in production: MESSAGE_DELTA, MESSAGE_END, METADATA, ERROR, HEARTBEAT. Each recorded entry stores: iso8601 timestamp, kind, payload (string), token_index (int optional), and consumer_side_marker (e.g., checkpoint id). Keep schema extensible but stable for equality checks.

Performance: recordings are compact JSONL files (one event per line) with optional gzip for long sessions. Replayer supports a deterministic RNG seed for any synthetic data generation so tests are reproducible.

Security: recordings may contain user content; by default the Recorder redacts payloads unless env var ALLOW_RECORD_PII is set. The harness documents safe storage for fixtures and recommends ephemeral test-only buckets.
api_examples:
Example: record a live session:

from redwood_sdk import ChatClient
from redwood_sdk.replay import Recorder

client = ChatClient(api_key=...)
rec = Recorder(record_file="fixtures/session-001.jsonl")

with rec.patch_client(client):
    resp = client.chat.stream(messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the quarterly report"}])
    async for ev in resp:
        # application logic that normally handles stream events
        pass

Replaying in a pytest fixture:

from redwood_sdk.replay import Replayer

@pytest.fixture
def session_fixture():
    return Replayer.from_file("fixtures/session-001.jsonl")

async def test_resume_on_disconnect(session_fixture):
    # Replayer can inject a disconnect at 1.2s and resume after backoff
    session_fixture.inject_error(at_seconds=1.2, kind="network")
    async for ev in session_fixture.stream():
        # assert handler sees same sequence of normalized events
        pass

Notes: Replayer.stream() yields the same event objects our public async iterator yields, allowing tests to use identical assertion logic. Clock and speedup arguments let CI run long recordings in milliseconds for fast feedback.
tradeoffs: Recording fidelity vs test determinism: capturing exact millisecond timing increases fidelity but makes tests sensitive to scheduling; mitigated by speedup factors and clock abstraction.
Not using production internals reduces coupling and increases portability, but may miss subtle runtime-only bugs (we keep a few golden recordings captured from canary infra to cover that).
Redaction by default avoids PII leaks but may require developers to opt-in to full recordings for deep debugging.
progress_updates: 2026-02-25: Ticket created. Initial API sketch shared in #sdk-streaming. Assigned to Miguel.
2026-02-27: Prototype Recorder implemented that writes JSONL with timestamps. First recording of a local dev session captured (sanitized).
2026-03-03: Replayer prototype can replay events with preserved inter-event timing and supports speedup factor. Added deterministic RNG for synthetic heartbeats.
2026-03-08: Added cancel token API and ensured Replayer can simulate abrupt disconnects and resumptions. WIP tests added to reproduce previous flaky integration test.
2026-03-10: Security review notes: default redact enabled; must add guidance for storing fixtures if they contain PII. Preparing PR for review.
open_questions: Should we expose Recorder.patch_client() as public helper or ship as a separate test-only package?
Do we standardize on JSONL as the golden fixture format or protobuf for compactness?
Where should canonical fixtures live (repo vs private S3)? Recommend private S3 with scripted sync into CI cache.
